subject: Community Medicine
concept: Blood-borne infections are infections transmitted through exposure to infected blood or specific body fluids; major public-health examples include HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C.

content.definition: Blood-borne infections are communicable infections for which infected blood or relevant body-fluid exposure can transmit the pathogen.
content.explanation: Public-health prevention combines safe blood systems, vaccination where available, injection and sharps safety, infection-prevention measures, testing and linkage to care, and prevention of mother-to-child transmission.
content.mechanism: Transmission occurs when infectious material reaches susceptible tissue, commonly through transfusion of contaminated blood, contaminated needles or sharps, sexual exposure for infections with relevant genital-fluid transmission, or vertical transmission.
content.clinical_relevance: Healthcare workers and patients can be exposed through unsafe injections, sharps injuries and inadequately processed equipment. Community programmes therefore need both source control and exposure prevention.
content.diagnosis: Population programmes use validated testing strategies and linkage to confirmatory testing or care according to the pathogen and national algorithm. A positive screening result should not automatically be treated as a final diagnosis when confirmatory testing is required.
content.treatment: Public-health treatment is pathogen-specific and should be linked to prevention: effective HIV antiretroviral therapy reduces onward sexual transmission; chronic HBV can be treated with oral antivirals in eligible patients; HCV is curable with direct-acting antivirals.
high_yield: Hepatitis B is vaccine-preventable; WHO recommends a birth dose as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours.
All donated blood should be screened for relevant transfusion-transmissible infections according to national and WHO standards.
Standard precautions treat blood and relevant body fluids as potentially infectious.
Needle-stick and sharps injuries require immediate occupational assessment and pathogen-specific post-exposure management when indicated.
Safe injection practice, sterilization or appropriate single-use equipment, and sharps disposal are core prevention measures.
For infants under 18 months exposed to HIV, virological testing is required because antibody testing alone is insufficient.

yemen_context.relevance: Blood safety, injection safety, vaccination, infection prevention and access to testing are relevant public-health priorities in Yemen.
yemen_context.evidence: WHO Yemen country strategy identifies infectious-disease surveillance and WASH/infection prevention among health-system priorities; no Yemen-specific blood-borne infection prevalence is asserted.

review_notes: Original synthesis based on WHO 2026 hepatitis guidance, WHO HIV guidance and WHO infection-prevention guidance.
